summary: The descriptive, spatial and inequality analyses are sound and robust: the burden is overwhelmingly concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, strongly spatially clustered (Moran's I 0.71 NTDs, 0.79 malaria; robust to weights specification and to restricting to LMICs or endemic countries) and concentrated in low-SDI settings.

Two substantive errors were found in the first-round scenario model and have been corrected (age-standardised rates multiplied by population; incomplete 2010 cause coverage). Corrected reference-scenario estimates: NTDs 241 thousand excess DALYs/year (95% UI 192–318), previously 394 thousand; malaria 1.85 million (1.51–2.21), previously 1.17 million.

The cross-sectional regression (first round) suggested that higher donor share was associated with 13% lower NTD burden per 10 percentage points. The panel analysis shows this is a between-country association: within countries over 2007–2022 the preferred two-way fixed-effects estimate is -0.64% (95% CI -2.39 to 1.14). The manuscript must therefore not claim that past donor financing measurably reduced NTD burden within countries; the scenario results rest on an explicit attribution assumption, not on an estimated causal effect.

For malaria, the preferred estimator suggests that a 10-point higher external share is associated with -6.32% (95% CI -10.85 to -1.56) burden, but this is not robust to cluster-robust errors, first differences or country-specific trends; report as suggestive.

Machine learning added no predictive value once leakage was removed: under leave-country-out validation LightGBM RMSE 0.52 vs elastic net 0.51; for forecasting, two-way FE RMSE 0.16 beat LightGBM 0.24. Random k-fold (R² 0.99) is spurious and must not be reported as performance.

Multiscale GWR shows UHC and sanitation act globally and protectively, whereas the external-financing association is local and changes sign (significant in 25% of countries), which explains the null pooled estimate and is itself a publishable heterogeneity finding.

methods: We conducted an ecological, multi-level spatial–econometric analysis of 204 countries and territories grouped into the seven GBD super-regions. Outcomes were age-standardised and all-age DALY rates for 19 neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) and malaria from GBD 2023, analysed annually from 2005 to 2023. Health-financing exposures (external, domestic government and out-of-pocket shares of current health expenditure) and development covariates came from the World Bank World Development Indicators; SDI, UHC effective coverage and lag-distributed income came from GBD 2023. WHO-reported people requiring NTD interventions (SDG 3.3.5) served as an independent outcome.

Burden was summarised by super-region with GBD 95% uncertainty intervals. Socioeconomic inequality was quantified with population-weighted concentration indices ranked by SDI (bootstrap 95% CI, 2 000 resamples) and a population-weighted Theil T decomposed into between- and within-super-region components.

Global spatial autocorrelation was assessed with Moran's I and local clusters with LISA (row-standardised k = 6 nearest-neighbour weights on projected centroids; 9 999 conditional permutations; Benjamini–Hochberg FDR q < .05). Sensitivity analyses varied k (4, 8) and used a 2 500 km inverse-distance band, and restricted the sample to LMICs and malaria-endemic countries.

The primary model was a two-way (country and year) fixed-effects regression of the log age-standardised DALY rate on the external share of current health expenditure (per 10 percentage points, lagged two years), adjusting for log domestic government health expenditure per capita (lag 2), log LDI, UHC index, and basic sanitation and drinking-water coverage, in LMICs 2007–2022 (malaria: malaria-endemic LMICs). Estimator choice was guided by Breusch–Pagan LM, Hausman and cluster-robust Mundlak tests. Given evidence of cross-sectional dependence (Pesaran CD), serial correlation (Wooldridge) and groupwise heteroskedasticity (modified Wald), we report Driscoll–Kraay standard errors. Robustness analyses included pooled OLS, random effects, correlated random effects, first differences, fixed effects with country-specific linear trends, and spatial lag and spatial error fixed-effects panel models.

Spatially varying relationships were examined with geographically weighted regression and multiscale GWR (adaptive bisquare kernel, AICc bandwidth selection, family-wise corrected inference). Random forest, LightGBM and elastic-net models were compared with panel models using leave-country-out, leave-one-super-region-out (spatial block) and temporal (train ≤2017, test 2018–2023) cross-validation; random k-fold results are reported only to illustrate leakage. SHAP values summarised feature importance.

Two complementary estimators projected excess annual DALYs under mild (5–15%), reference (19–26%, bracketing the IHME-estimated 22% decline in development assistance for health, 2024–2025) and severe (40–60%) cuts. The accounting model attributes the 2010–2023 reduction in all-age DALY rates to external financing in proportion to the external share of health expenditure, and reverses that share by the cut magnitude, applied to 2023 populations. The econometric model applies the preferred fixed-effects coefficient to the cut-induced fall in external share. Uncertainty combined GBD draws (rank-correlated across years), cut magnitude, and coefficient sampling (4 000 Monte Carlo draws). Health losses were valued at 0.5, 1 and 3 times GDP per capita per DALY. The domestic financing gap was expressed as the increase in domestic government health spending required to replace lost external funds.
Python 3.13: pandas, statsmodels, linearmodels, PySAL (libpysal, esda, spreg, mgwr), scikit-learn, LightGBM, SHAP, GeoPandas, matplotlib. All code and processed data are provided.
limits: Ecological design: associations at country level cannot be interpreted for individuals.
GBD estimates are modelled, smoothed, and partly covariate-driven, which attenuates within-country associations and creates partial circularity with GBD-derived covariates.

No country-level, NTD-specific development assistance series was available in this analysis (IHME DAH by health focus area); external share of total health expenditure is an imperfect proxy and probably understates NTD-programme dependence.
No valid instrument or natural experiment for donor financing; estimates are associational. The 2025 cuts themselves may provide a natural experiment once post-2025 data are released.
Scenario estimates assume proportional attribution and steady-state reversal; disease-specific transmission dynamics and drug-donation continuity are not modelled.
Sub-national heterogeneity (e.g. focal NTD transmission) is masked at country level.
legends: Figure 1. Analytical workflow from data acquisition to outputs.

Five public data sources feed a harmonised country-year panel (stages 1–3). Three analytic tracks branch from it: descriptive and inequality analysis (stage 4), spatial analysis (stage 5) and panel econometrics (stage 6). Panel results feed the robustness and heterogeneity models (stage 7) and the funding-cut scenario models (stage 8), which use the preferred coefficient from stage 6. Outputs are Tables 1–4, Tables S1–S13 and Figures 1–8.
